etymologies.etymologyHTML: Recorded in Middle English since circa 1225, borrowed from Old French consentir, from Latin cōnsentīre (“to agree; to assent, consent”), itself from com- (“with”) + sentiō (“to feel”)

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To express willingness, to give permission.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: My poverty, but not my will, consents.

definitions.definition: (transitive, medicine) To cause to sign a consent form.

quote.citation: 2002, T Usmani with KD O'Brien, HV Worthington, S Derwent, et al., “A randomized clinical trial to compare the effectiveness of canine lacebacks with reference to canine tip”, in Journal of Orthodontics, volume 29, number 4, →DOI, →PMID:
quote.text: When the patient was consented to enter the study and registered, a telephone call was made to research assistant

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To grant; to allow; to assent to.

quote.citation: 1644, J[ohn] M[ilton], The Doctrine or Discipline of Divorce: […], 2nd edition, London: [s.n.], →OCLC, book:
quote.text: Interpreters  […]  will not consent it to be a true story.

definitions.definition: To agree in opinion or sentiment; to be of the same mind; to accord; to concur.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 8:1:
quote.text: And Saul was consenting unto his death.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: Flourishing many years before Wyclif, and much consenting with him in judgment.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 6, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: All men know by experience, there be some parts of our bodies which often without any consent of ours doe stirre, stand, and lye down againe.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Unity or agreement of opinion, sentiment, or inclination.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 14:18:
quote.text: And they all with one consent began to make excuse.
